summary:
Beyond Earth 2.0 is an interactive tool that compares terrain on Mars with locations on Earth using real NASA elevation data. Our project uses Mars Orbiter Laser Altimeter (MOLA) and Shuttle Radar Topography Mission (SRTM) data to measure terrain slope, elevation variation, and surface roughness.

We developed a reproducible matching algorithm that compares five Earth regions with Jezero Crater on Mars and ranks them by terrain similarity. Aljojuca ranks first, followed by Lake Salda, Lonar, Makgadikgadi, and Western Lake Eyre.

Our interactive website allows users to explore the ranked locations, examine maps, and understand the measurements behind each comparison.

The project helps researchers identify promising locations for further investigation while acknowledging that terrain similarity alone cannot establish geological equivalence or landing suitability.
details:
Beyond Earth 2.0: Earth–Mars Terrain Explorer

The Problem

Researchers studying Mars need accessible Earth locations where they can investigate comparable terrain and test scientific approaches. However, visual resemblance alone cannot establish terrain similarity or geological equivalence.

Our Solution

Beyond Earth 2.0 is an interactive web application that compares a 60 × 60 km region around Jezero Crater on Mars with five selected Earth locations.

The application displays ranked Earth candidates, an interactive geographic map, a Mars terrain visualization, and detailed comparisons explaining why each location received its score.

NASA Data

We use two primary elevation datasets:

  • NASA Mars Orbiter Laser Altimeter (MOLA), collected by Mars Global Surveyor.
  • NASA/NGA Shuttle Radar Topography Mission (SRTMGL1), distributed through OpenTopography.

Both datasets are processed using a shared regional comparison protocol with 1 km grid cells.

Matching Algorithm

Our algorithm compares three terrain characteristics:

  1. Mean terrain slope.
  2. Elevation standard deviation.
  3. Local surface roughness, measured using plane-fit residuals.

A deterministic weighted-distance formula combines their normalized differences into a relative similarity score.

Results

We measured and ranked five Earth regions against Jezero:

  1. Aljojuca, Mexico — 0.763346
  2. Lake Salda, Türkiye — 0.662219
  3. Lonar, India — 0.562146
  4. Makgadikgadi, Botswana — 0.520936
  5. Western Lake Eyre, Australia — 0.517456

These scores describe relative terrain similarity among the selected candidates. They are not probabilities of scientific or operational suitability.

Implementation

The scientific pipeline uses Python, NumPy, SciPy, Rasterio, and related geospatial tools.

The frontend uses JavaScript and provides interactive maps, linked candidate selection, terrain comparisons, and transparent source information.

The implementation passed 36 automated tests, scientific validation checks, and local browser verification. The application is publicly deployed.

Innovation and Impact

Our approach combines reproducible NASA elevation measurements with an explainable ranking system. Users can inspect individual terrain features rather than relying on an unexplained similarity score.

The project can help researchers prioritize Earth locations for further geological investigation and instrument experiments.

Limitations

Our prototype compares one Mars reference with five preselected Earth regions. It does not perform a global search.

Terrain similarity does not establish matching geology, mineralogy, water history, landing safety, or mission suitability. Different source resolutions, interpolation, smoothing, and initial scoring weights can influence the results.

Future development could include additional Mars locations, more Earth candidates, higher-resolution measurements, uncertainty analysis, and geological evidence.
